searchText: Lecture 7: Number Formats and Quantization — Worked Mathematics Efficient AI · Lecture 7 · deep undergraduate mathematics Lecture 7: Number Formats and Quantization A finite bit pattern is a promise about which numbers a machine can represent. Learn to read that promise, calculate its error, and explain why more range and more precision compete for the same bits. Open the supplied numeric-format review ↗ Based on the Lecture 7 material appended to Mid-term Review.pdf, pages 83–98 . Slide examples are marked; additional problems and affine-quantization derivations are constructed practice. [Review, pages 83–85] Priority practice: the review’s yellow-star topics include integer interpretation, FP32 encoding, zero/subnormal handling, special exponent patterns, and the low-bit range/precision comparison. The full-deck star audit lives with the main midterm guide. Page numbers here refer to PDF pages, not a newly invented lecture numbering scheme. Real value What must be stored? Choose format Range and step size Encode bits Integer or float Decode and compare Representation error A bit budget controls the available codebook; decoding tells you what a stored code actually means. 1 · Integer codes 2 · Fixed point 3 · Floating point 4 · FP32 encoding 5 · FP16 decoding 6 · Small numbers 7 · Special patterns 8 · Precision 9 · Low-bit formats 10 · Quantization 11 · Error and storage 12 · Mixed exam practice 1 · Bits do not identify a number until the representation is known Start with 11000000 , the review’s integer exercise. Reading it as unsigned gives 192. Reading the first bit as a sign and the remaining seven as a magnitude gives −64. Reading it as two’s complement also gives −64. The last two happen to agree for this pattern, so this example alone cannot teach you how to distinguish those representations. The preceding source page explicitly names sign-magnitude under its “signed integer” heading. [Review, pages 83–84] Let n be the bit width and b i the bit at position i , counting from the right starting at 0. Each bit is 0 or 1. Unsigned decoding is simply a weighted sum of powers of two: u = Σ i=0 n−1 b i 2 i For eight bits, positions weigh 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Thus 11000000 means 128 + 64 = 192. The unsigned range is 0 through 2 n − 1 because all-one bits add to the geometric sum 1 + 2 + … + 2 n−1 . In sign-magnitude , the first bit s contributes a sign, not an additional magnitude digit. Decode the remaining n−1 bits as a nonnegative integer m , then compute (−1) s m . Its range is −(2 n−1 − 1) through +(2 n−1 − 1); two codes represent zero. For 11000000 , s = 1 and the magnitude 1000000 is 64, hence −64. In two’s complement , the leftmost bit has negative place value. All other positions retain their usual positive place values: v = −b n−1 2 n−1 + Σ i=0 n−2 b i 2 i The eight-bit pattern therefore gives −128 + 64 = −64. There is one zero, and the range is −128 through 127. Another decoding route is useful: first compute unsigned u ; if the top bit is 1, subtract 2 n . Here 192 − 256 = −64. This is the same formula because changing the top position from +128 to −128 subtracts 256. Worked variant: one pattern, three different answers Interpret 10110110 in all three schemes. Unsigned: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182 . Sign-magnitude: minus (32 + 16 + 4 + 2) = −54 . Two’s complement: −128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −74 . The difference is a decoding rule, not a change in the stored bits. Practice 1 · Similar formula, different pattern Decode 11100101 as unsigned, sign-magnitude, and two’s complement. Show the place values before giving the three results. Worked explanation Unsigned is 128 + 64 + 32 + 4 + 1 = 229 . Sign-magnitude excludes the sign bit from the magnitude: −(64 + 32 + 4 + 1) = −101 . Two’s complement is 229 − 256 = −27 . A negative sign by itself does not tell you which signed representation is intended. On an exam, write the representation next to the answer; “signed” alone is too vague unless the question defines its convention. For this review, its explicitly labeled sign-magnitude branch supplies the intended meaning. Do not assume that every signed format is sign-magnitude or that the review’s accidental equal answers establish equivalence. 2 · Fixed point moves the binary point without changing the stored integer The review encodes 00110001 in an eight-bit, two’s-complement format with four fractional bits. The bit pattern has integer value 49. Scaling by 2 −4 makes its represented real value 49/16 = 3.0625 . The slide shows the direct fractional-place-value route and this integer-then-scale route side by side. [Review, page 85] Let v be the signed stored integer and f the number of fractional bits. Define the real represented value x̂ , read “x hat,” by x̂ = v × 2 −f The binary point is a convention shared by all values in this format; no separate exponent is stored with each value. Adjacent integers differ by 1, so adjacent represented reals differ by Δ = 2 −f . For f = 4, the step is 1/16 = 0.0625. The eight-bit range becomes −128/16 through 127/16, or −8 through 7.9375 . Trace the review’s value in both directions Place the binary point as 0011.0001 . The leading bit has weight −2³; the other integer positions have weights 2², 2¹, 2⁰. The fractional positions have weights 2 −1 , 2 −2 , 2 −3 , 2 −4 . The nonzero entries contribute 2 + 1 + 1/16 = 3.0625. Alternatively, 00110001 is 32 + 16 + 1 = 49; 49 × 2 −4 gives the same result. Worked variant: decode a negative fixed-point value With the same eight-bit/four-fractional-bit convention, 11010110 has unsigned value 214. Two’s-complement integer value is 214 − 256 = −42. Divide by 16: x̂ = −2.625 . Direct place values also work: −8 + 4 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.125 = −2.625. Applying the sign only to the fractional tail would be wrong; the negative top-bit weight applies to the entire integer decoding. Encoding reverses the operation. Given desired x , choose an integer close to x 2 f . This workbook uses rounding to nearest with ties to even and clipping to the allowed integer range when necessary; the source fixed-point slide defines the representation but does not specify a rounding policy. These rounding/clipping exercises are constructed extensions. Practice 2 · Encode exactly, then quantify an approximation In the same format, encode 1.6875. Next encode 1.7 using the stated rounding policy. Give the stored integer, bits, represented value, and signed error x̂ − x. Worked explanation For 1.6875, multiply by 16: 27 exactly. Integer 27 is 00011011 ; decoding gives 27/16 = 1.6875 with zero error. For 1.7, multiply by 16: 27.2. Nearest integer is 27, giving the same bits and represented value. Error is 1.6875 − 1.7 = −0.0125 . Its absolute size 0.0125 is below the unsaturated nearest-rounding limit Δ/2 = 0.03125. Keeping eight total bits but increasing f from 4 to 6 shrinks the step from 1/16 to 1/64. The range also shrinks to −2 through 127/64 = 1.984375. This is a concrete range/precision tradeoff: the former exactly represented value 3.0625 no longer fits. A smaller step is useful only if the values you need are still inside the range. 3 · A normal floating-point value combines a significand and a scale Floating point stores a sign, an exponent field, and a fraction field. A binary32 value uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. The review normalizes its example 0.265625 as 1.0625 × 2 −2 ; the exponent determines the scale and the significand determines the position within that scale. [Review, pages 86–87] Use consistent notation: s is the sign bit; e the exponent-field width; m the fraction-field width; E the exponent field interpreted as an unsigned integer; F the fraction field interpreted as an unsigned integer. The mathematical fraction is F /2 m . The exponent bias is β = 2 e−1 − 1 . For binary32, β = 127; for binary16, β = 15. x = (−1) s (1 + F/2 m )2 E−β Normal finite values: 1 ≤ E ≤ 2 e − 2 The initial 1 of a normalized binary significand is not stored. For example, binary 1.101 has significand value 1 + 1/2 + 1/8 = 1.625. The stored fraction begins 101 and contributes 0.625. This hidden leading bit is why a normal binary32 number has 24 significant binary digits despite having only 23 fraction-field bits. The bias does not change the represented exponent; it changes how that exponent is stored. If the real power is −2, the binary32 exponent field stores E = −2 + 127 = 125 . To decode, subtract the bias and recover −2. The source motivates bias as a way to store negative and positive exponents in a nonnegative bit field. [Review, page 87] 1 | 10001 | 1100000000 sign | stored exponent | stored fraction The review’s FP16 example: the fields are read separately before the value is reconstructed. These formulas are for normal finite numbers. A zero exponent field switches to the zero/subnormal rule, and an all-one exponent field switches to infinity/NaN. Those cases are part of the decoding contract, not optional corrections. The source headings that say “Exponent ≠ 0” must be read together with its later special-pattern table; they do not imply all-one exponents are normal. [Review, pages 92–93] 4 · Encoding a decimal value means normalizing its binary expansion The starred source example: encode 0.265625 in binary32 Make the fraction exact. 0.265625 = 17/64 = 1/4 + 1/64, so binary is 0.010001 . Normalize. Move the point two places right: 1.0001 × 2⁻² . The significand is 1 + 1/16 = 1.0625. Encode sign. The number is positive, so s = 0. Encode exponent. Real exponent is −2; stored exponent is 125. Its eight-bit binary pattern is 01111101 . Encode fraction. Drop the hidden leading 1. Store 0001 and pad with zeroes to 23 bits: 00010000000000000000000 . Check by decoding. (1 + 1/16)2 125−127 = (17/16)/4 = 17/64 = 0.265625 . 0 | 01111101 | 00010000000000000000000 The review gives this exact normalized value and field interpretation; the step-by-step binary decomposition above makes its arithmetic explicit. There is no rounding error because 17/64 has a finite binary expansion that fits well within the field width. [Review, page 86] Practice 3 · Encode −6.5 with the same difficulty Give binary32 sign, exponent field, fraction field, and a reverse calculation proving your answer. Worked explanation Magnitude 6.5 = binary 110.1 = 1.101 × 2² . Sign is 1. Stored exponent is 2 + 127 = 129 = 10000001 . The fraction 101 means 1/2 + 1/8 = 0.625; pad to 23 bits. Fields are 1 | 10000001 | 10100000000000000000000 . Reverse calculation is −(1 + 0.625)2² = −6.5 . Do not store 6 as the exponent: the exponent is a power, not the integer part of the original value. For a number whose binary expansion does not terminate within the available fraction bits, you need a rounding rule. You cannot merely discard bits and claim the stored value is exact. This workbook separates exact source-style encoding questions from explicitly rounded extensions so that the question supplies enough information to give one answer. 5 · FP16 changes the field widths, not the method Binary16 uses 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 10 fraction bits. Its bias is 15. The review asks you to decode 1 | 10001 | 1100000000 . The first task is to keep the field boundaries intact; treating the full 16-bit pattern as an ordinary signed integer answers a different question. [Review, pages 94–95] The source’s −7 calculation Sign 1 gives a negative value. Exponent 10001 is 17, so real exponent is 17 − 15 = 2. Fraction 1100000000 is 1/2 + 1/4 = 0.75, not integer 110 and not 768 as a real fraction. The significand is 1.75. Therefore x = −1.75 × 2² = −7 . Alternatively, fraction integer F = 768; F/1024 = 0.75 gives the same result. Practice 4 · A new FP16 normal value Decode 0 | 10000 | 0110000000 . Explain what each field contributes. Worked explanation Sign is positive. E = 16, so the scale is 2 16−15 = 2. The fraction is 0/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8 = 0.375. Thus x = (1 + 0.375)2 = 2.75 . A wrong answer 0.75 forgets the hidden leading 1. Practice 5 · Encode a small negative FP16 value Encode −0.15625 exactly. Give the exponent and fraction fields, then decode to check. Worked explanation Magnitude 0.15625 = 5/32 = binary 0.00101 = 1.01 × 2⁻³ . Sign is 1. Stored exponent is −3 + 15 = 12 = 01100 . Fraction is 1/4 = 0.25, so store 0100000000 . Fields: 1 | 01100 | 0100000000 . Decoding gives −(1 + 0.25)2 −3 = −1.25/8 = −0.15625 . Writing the field widths explicitly prevents a common transfer mistake: subtracting the binary32 bias 127 from an FP16 exponent. A format name controls the bias and bit boundaries together. A 16-bit storage width alone is insufficient because BF16 has different exponent/fraction widths. 6 · Subnormals fill the gap between zero and the smallest normal value If the normal formula always included a leading 1, setting the fraction to zero would still leave a nonzero significand. The review therefore changes the rule when E = 0: remove the hidden 1 and use a fixed exponent 1 − β. This yields zero when the fraction is zero and a sequence of small nonzero values when it is not. [Review, pages 88–89] x = (−1) s (F/2 m )2 1−β ,   E = 0 The exponent is 1 − β , not 0 − β . This choice makes the gap from the largest subnormal to the smallest normal exactly one subnormal step. To see why, let the smallest positive subnormal have fraction integer F = 1. Its value is δ = 2 1−β−m Subnormals are integer multiples Fδ for 1 ≤ F ≤ 2 m − 1. The smallest positive normal has E = 1 and F = 0, giving 2 1−β = 2 m δ. The largest subnormal is therefore one δ below it: largest positive subnormal = (1 − 2 −m )2 1−β = smallest positive normal − δ The review’s binary32 boundary For β = 127 and m = 23, smallest subnormal is 2 −149 . Smallest normal is 2 −126 . Largest subnormal has all 23 fraction bits set to 1, giving (1 − 2 −23 )2 −126 = 2 −126 − 2 −149 . This is the review’s displayed result. Keep the powers exact: writing a rounded decimal for both boundary values can hide the tiny difference. [Review, pages 90–91] Practice 6 · Transfer the same boundary derivation to FP16 Find the smallest positive subnormal, smallest positive normal, and largest positive subnormal for binary16. Give exact powers and the boundary gap. Worked explanation With β = 15 and m = 10, δ = 2 1−15−10 = 2 −24 . Smallest normal is 2 −14 . Largest subnormal is (1 − 2 −10 )2 −14 = 2 −14 − 2 −24 . The gap is exactly 2 −24 . This derivation changes field widths while preserving the source’s reasoning. Practice 7 · Decode a subnormal instead of a normal Decode FP16 0 | 00000 | 0000000011 . Why is using 1 + fraction wrong? Worked explanation E = 0 triggers the subnormal branch. Fraction integer is F = 3; value is (3/1024)2 −14 = 3 × 2 −24 . Adding a hidden 1 would jump to a different scale and destroy the intended small-value encoding. The question is the same decoding task as Practice 4, but the exponent branch changes the formula. Subnormal steps have constant absolute spacing δ. As values approach zero, that same absolute step becomes a larger fraction of the value. Consequently the relative precision available near zero declines. This is a mathematical consequence of Fδ; it does not by itself tell you whether any particular accelerator executes subnormal arithmetic normally or flushes it to zero. 7 · Classify the exponent before doing arithmetic The source reserves the all-one exponent field for infinities and NaNs. A zero fraction then means infinity; a nonzero fraction means NaN , “not a number.” The sign distinguishes +∞ and −∞; a NaN bit pattern does not encode an ordinary real number with a usable magnitude. [Review, pages 92–93] Exponent field Fraction field Interpretation Formula / action E = 0 F = 0 Signed zero Sign selects +0 or −0 E = 0 F > 0 Subnormal (−1)ˢ(F/2ᵐ)2¹⁻ᵝ 1 ≤ E ≤ 2ᵉ−2 Any F Normal finite (−1)ˢ(1+F/2ᵐ)2ᴱ⁻ᵝ E = 2ᵉ−1 F = 0 Infinity +∞ or −∞ E = 2ᵉ−1 F > 0 NaN Classify; no finite decimal value The largest finite normal binary32 number must use E = 254, not 255. Its fraction is all ones, so the significand is 2 − 2 −23 and the value is (2 − 2 −23 )2 127 . For binary16, use E = 30 and m = 10; the largest finite value is (2 − 2 −10 )2 15 = 65504 . These are constructed applications of the source’s special-pattern table, not added measurements. Practice 8 · A short conceptual classification question For FP16, classify the fields below without forcing every pattern through the normal formula: A 0|00000|0000000000 ; B 1|00000|0000000000 ; C 0|11111|0000000000 ; D 1|11111|0000000001 . Worked explanation A is +0 ; B is −0 ; C is +∞ ; D is NaN . D is not “negative infinity” because its fraction is nonzero. The visible sign bit does not turn a NaN into a finite negative number. The right first move is classification by E and F. All-zero and all-one exponent fields are branch conditions; check them before subtracting a bias and inserting a leading 1. Also distinguish the exponent field from the numerical exponent: a real exponent of zero corresponds to a normal value whose stored exponent equals the bias. 8 · Fraction bits determine local spacing; exponent bits determine reachable scales The review compares FP32 (8 exponent/23 fraction), FP16 (5/10), and BF16 (8/7), emphasizing range versus precision. FP16 and BF16 both use 16 bits, but BF16 spends more of them on exponent range while FP16 spends more on fraction precision. This comparison concerns their represented values, not an automatic ranking of model accuracy or runtime. [Review, page 94] Within a normal binary interval [2 k , 2 k+1 ), increasing the fraction integer F by one increases the significand by 2 −m . Multiplying by 2 k gives the spacing ULP in [2 k , 2 k+1 ) = 2 k−m ULP means “unit in the last place,” the local spacing between adjacent representable normal values. This derivation is an extension of the source field-width comparison. It explains why floating-point spacing grows with magnitude: multiplying by a larger scale enlarges the same fraction-field step. Worked spacing comparison at 1 At the start of [1, 2), k = 0. Binary32 spacing is 2 −23 ; binary16 spacing is 2 −10 = 1/1024 ; BF16 spacing is 2 −7 = 1/128 . BF16 spacing here is eight times FP16 spacing. Around magnitude 8, binary16 has k = 3 and spacing 2 3−10 = 1/128 = 0.0078125 . FP16 has not lost fraction bits; its exponent scale made the absolute step larger. Practice 9 · Rounding is a format-plus-policy question Consider FP16 at 1. The next value is 1 + 2 −10 . Under nearest, ties-to-even rounding, where does x = 1 + 2 −11 go? Explain why an answer requires the rounding rule. Worked explanation x is exactly halfway between 1 and 1 + 2 −10 . At the lower value, the fraction integer F = 0 is even; at the upper value F = 1 is odd. Ties-to-even chooses 1 . A different tie rule could choose differently. The signed error is −2 −11 , exactly minus half the spacing. This policy is stated for the exercise; it is not specified by the review’s field-width picture. More exponent bits can prevent overflow for a wider magnitude range, but do not guarantee better resolution around a given number. More fraction bits reduce local rounding error, but do not prevent overflow if the exponent range is too small. Useful answers name the value distribution and the failure being prevented instead of simply saying one format is “more accurate.” FP8 also needs a specific convention, not just an eight-bit width Page96 gives two NVIDIA FP8 examples: E4M3 has one sign bit, four exponent bits, and three fraction bits; E5M2 has one sign bit, five exponent bits, and two fraction bits. The source explicitly says its E4M3 example has no infinity encoding, uses sign|1111|111 for NaN, and has largest finite positive pattern 0|1111|110 with value 448 . Its E5M2 example reserves sign|11111|00 for infinity and nonzero fraction at that exponent for NaN, with maximum finite positive pattern 0|11110|11 equal to 57344 . [Review, page 96] Explain the two maximum-value calculations For the illustrated E4M3 convention, bias 7 and fraction110 give significand 1 +1/2+1/4=1.75; stored exponent 15 gives real exponent 8. Thus 1.75×2⁸= 448 . The largest exponent field still contains finite encodings in this convention; only the specified fraction 111 at that field is NaN. For the illustrated E5M2 convention, bias 15 and fraction11 give 1.75; exponent 30 gives real exponent 15. Thus 1.75×2¹⁵= 57344 . Exponent31 is unavailable for normal finite values because it is the infinity/NaN branch. The bias values here are the conventions consistent with the slide’s named patterns and results; the maximum-value arithmetic is an explanatory derivation. Practice · Compare two FP8 designs without copying FP32 rules A question describes precisely the two source conventions. Which has the larger maximum finite magnitude? Which devotes more bits to resolving the significand? Why would classifying every all-one exponent as infinity/NaN fail for one of them? Model explanation E5M2 reaches 57344 , larger than E4M3’s 448 . E4M3 uses three fraction bits instead of two, so at a shared normal scale it has finer fraction resolution. The source’s E4M3 convention retains finite encodings at exponent 1111; the specified fraction 111 gives NaN and there is no infinity. An unqualified IEEE-binary32 special-case rule would misclassify valid E4M3 numbers. The format’s documented contract controls decoding. 9 · Low-bit formats use different codebooks, even with the same four-bit budget The starred low-bit comparison shows INT4 beside FP4 E1M2, E2M1, and E3M0. “E1M2” means one exponent bit and two fraction bits in addition to one sign bit; the other names describe the same allocation rule. These source examples are their own finite low-bit conventions. Do not transplant binary32’s infinity reservation without checking the format. The source lists finite maximum values 3.5, 6, and 16 for these FP4 illustrations. [Review, pages 96–97] Source illustration Nonnegative codebook What it favors INT4 two’s complement 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 Uniform integer spacing; negative side includes −8 FP4 E1M2 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 More dense values over a narrower range FP4 E2M1 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 Intermediate exponent reach and precision FP4 E3M0 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 Large range; very coarse spacing at high magnitudes The table transcribes the slide’s positive-side sets. The FP4 illustrations also have negative sign counterparts and signed zero. The review uses zero-exponent subnormal behavior for the E1M2/E2M1 examples and permits finite all-one exponent fields; these are not IEEE binary16 or binary32 encodings. Trace three source FP4 patterns E1M2 0|0|01 : source subnormal formula is 0.25 × 2¹ = 0.5 . Its maximum positive 0|1|11 is (1 + 0.75)2¹ = 3.5 . E2M1 0|00|1 : source subnormal formula gives 0.5 × 2⁰ = 0.5 . Maximum positive 0|11|1 gives (1 + 0.5)2 3−1 = 6 . E3M0 0|001 : no fraction bits remain, so positive finite values are powers of two. The source’s bias 3 gives 2 1−3 = 0.25 . At 0|111 , value is 2 7−3 = 16 . The stored exponent field uses all three remaining bits. Practice 10 · Reason from the source codebook Which source FP4 codebook represents 8 exactly? Which represents 2.5 exactly? Which would give the nearest nonnegative represented value to 2.6 if nearest rounding is used? Restrict your answer to the listed codebooks. Worked explanation Only E3M0 contains 8. Only E1M2 contains 2.5. For 2.6, E1M2 chooses 2.5 (distance 0.1); E2M1 chooses 3 (distance 0.4); E3M0 chooses 2 (distance 0.6). Thus E1M2 has the closest codebook value for this particular input. This does not prove it is best for a tensor containing values up to 16: its maximum 3.5 would force clipping or another scale. Scaled integers can imitate a fixed-step codebook: multiplying the integer set −8,…,7 by 0.5 gives −4,…,3.5. That set still differs from the sign-based E1M2 example, whose negative magnitudes mirror the positive magnitudes. The scale and the signed convention both matter; visual similarities between codebooks do not make the formats identical. 10 · Affine quantization chooses a scale and a zero point for an integer codebook The final source page defines quantization as mapping a continuous or large set of inputs to a discrete set and identifies quantization error as the difference between input and quantized value. It does not provide an affine neural-network quantizer formula. Everything in this section is therefore a constructed mathematical extension of that definition, with its assumptions supplied here. [Review, page 98] Assume an integer code q restricted to [ q min , q max ], a positive scale a , and an integer zero point z . Define dequantization, the reconstructed real value, by x̂ = a(q − z) The scale is the real spacing between adjacent integer codes. The zero point tells us which code means real zero: q = z gives x̂ = 0. Solving for the ideal real-valued code gives q* = x/a + z. It may not be an integer or may lie outside the code range, so encoding requires rounding and clipping: q = clip(round(x/a) + z, q min , q max ) Here round means nearest with ties to even; clip limits the result to the specified interval. The formula deliberately rounds x/a before adding z. At exact halfway ties, ties-to-even rounding of x/a + z can differ when z is odd, because shifting by an odd integer changes the parity of the adjacent codes. These choices make every practice answer deterministic; other quantizers may choose different conventions. For example, at x/a = 3.5 and z = 5, this formula gives round(3.5) + 5 = 9, while round(3.5 + 5) gives 8. State the order as well as the tie rule. Derive the endpoint scale and zero point Suppose you want q_min to reconstruct a minimum real value x_min and q_max to reconstruct x_max. The two equations are x_min = a(q_min − z) and x_max = a(q_max − z). Subtracting eliminates z: x_max − x_min = a(q_max − q_min). Therefore a = (x_max − x_min)/(q_max − q_min), assuming x_max > x_min. Solving the first equation gives z* = q_min − x_min/a. A practical integer zero point requires rounding and possibly clipping z*. If z* is not exactly an allowed integer, both endpoints need not reconstruct exactly after that adjustment. Constant-valued calibration data also need a separate scale rule because the difference x_max−x_min would be zero. Worked affine example: unsigned four-bit codes Take q_min = 0, q_max = 15, x_min = −2, x_max = 5.5. This is a constructed range, not a slide experiment. Endpoint scale is a = (5.5 − (−2))/15 = 7.5/15 = 0.5 . Ideal zero point is 0 − (−2)/0.5 = 4 , already an integer in the range. Reconstruction is x̂ = 0.5(q − 4); q = 0 gives −2, q = 15 gives 5.5, and q = 4 gives zero. Original x Round(x/a)+z Stored q x̂ x̂−x −1.3 round(−2.6)+4 = 1 1 −1.5 −0.2 0.3 round(0.6)+4 = 5 5 0.5 0.2 1.8 round(3.6)+4 = 8 8 2 0.2 6.2 round(12.4)+4 = 16 15 after clip 5.5 −0.7 The out-of-range input 6.2 demonstrates saturation : the endpoint code represents 5.5 even though a larger input arrived. Saturation error is a different mechanism from rounding between interior levels. Increasing the range while keeping the same code count increases the spacing, so it can reduce clipping while increasing ordinary rounding error. Practice 11 · Change the input without changing the quantizer Using a = 0.5, z = 4, and codes 0,…,15, quantize 1.1. State the ideal scaled input, stored code, reconstruction, and signed error. Worked explanation x/a = 1.1/0.5 = 2.2. Round to 2 and add 4: q = 6 . Reconstruction is 0.5(6 − 4) = 1 . Signed error is 1 − 1.1 = −0.1 . There is no clipping because q is inside the code interval. Practice 12 · Change the scale and encounter a tie An unsigned four-bit quantizer has a = 0.2 and z = 5. Quantize x = 0.7 using nearest, ties-to-even rounding. What changes if the question had instead specified ties upward? Worked explanation x/a = 3.5 exactly. The stated round-before-offset convention rounds 3.5 to 4, so q = 9 and x̂ = 0.2(9−5) = 0.8 . If a different question defined q = round(x/a + z), ties-to-even would round 8.5 to 8 and reconstruct 0.6; that is a different quantizer convention. Ties upward also chooses 4 here, so this particular result is unchanged. The tie policy still matters in general: a tie at 2.5 would round to 2 under ties-to-even and to 3 under upward ties. Do not claim this example proves tie rules always agree. A symmetric extension sets z = 0. For a four-bit illustration, choose codes −7,…,7 deliberately, leaving the two’s-complement −8 code unused, and cover real magnitudes through 3.5. Then a = 3.5/7 = 0.5. Input −1.2 gives round(−2.4) = −2 and reconstruction −1. This convention is common enough to motivate the mathematics but is not specified by the source’s INT4 picture; the unused code and scale are assumptions in our exercise. 11 · Representation error and model error are different measurements Define signed reconstruction error ε = x̂ − x. Its sign tells you whether the reconstruction is above or below the input; |ε| measures its magnitude. For unsaturated nearest rounding on a uniform grid of spacing a, the nearest code lies at most a/2 away. Therefore |ε| ≤ a/2 , provided clipping is inactive. This is a statement about this scalar quantizer, not about a neural network’s final accuracy. The three unsaturated worked affine inputs have errors −0.2, +0.2, +0.2. The mean squared error (MSE) is the average of squared errors: MSE = (0.2² + 0.2² + 0.2²)/3 = 0.04 The input 6.2 has absolute error 0.7, larger than a/2 = 0.25, because saturation is active. The half-step bound is not wrong; applying it outside its assumptions is wrong. Similarly, a small scalar MSE alone does not establish preserved task accuracy. Different parameters or activations can influence a model’s outputs differently. Low-bit storage can reduce the raw value bytes. For P stored values and bit width b , ideal packed storage is Pb/8 bytes. One million values need 4,000,000 bytes at 32 bits, 1,000,000 bytes at 8 bits, or 500,000 bytes at 4 bits. These are 4 MB, 1 MB, and 0.5 MB using decimal MB = 10⁶ bytes. The formula excludes scales, zero points, alignment, and other metadata. It also assumes four-bit packing rather than allocating a full byte per four-bit value. The arithmetic savings are constructed storage calculations. They do not establish a four-times speedup, an eight-times speedup, or a latency number. Actual performance depends on how the hardware and implementation store and execute the format, and on which part of the application dominates runtime. 12 · Mixed practice asks you to choose the formula before substituting These questions preserve the review’s sentiment: interpretation, basic calculation, and explaining what a format buys. They change the input values and require the same core reasoning; optional boundary and rounding questions are labeled extensions rather than silently raising the source example’s difficulty. Practice 13 · Conceptual, same difficulty Two formats both use 16 bits. Format A has 5 exponent and 10 fraction bits; format B has 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits. Which better preserves small differences around 1? Which reaches more exponent scales? State the tradeoff without claiming either guarantees better model accuracy. Model explanation A has more fraction bits, so its local spacing around 1 is 2⁻¹⁰ rather than B’s 2⁻⁷; it better resolves small differences there. B has a wider exponent field, so it reaches more scales. Neither fact alone specifies the distribution of the model’s values or its sensitivity to representation error, so it does not establish model accuracy. A complete answer connects each bit field to its own consequence. Practice 14 · Boundary reasoning extension A student says, “The largest FP16 subnormal equals the smallest FP16 normal because their decimals round to the same display.” Explain the mathematical error and give the exact gap. Model explanation The exact largest subnormal is (1−2⁻¹⁰)2⁻¹⁴ and the smallest normal is 2⁻¹⁴. Subtracting gives 2⁻²⁴ , a positive difference. A rounded display can conceal distinct bit-pattern values; it does not prove equality. Exact powers are preferable in boundary questions. Practice 15 · Quantization interpretation extension In x̂ = 0.5(q−4), a student says code 0 means real zero. Identify the error, give the code for zero, and explain why x = 6.2 does not satisfy the half-step error bound. Model explanation Code 0 reconstructs 0.5(0−4) = −2 . Real zero uses q = 4 . Input 6.2 needs an out-of-range code and is clipped to q = 15, giving x̂ = 5.5 and error −0.7. The half-step bound applies only to unsaturated nearest rounding, so it cannot be used for this input. Practice 16 · Short answer, same difficulty Why does increasing exponent width while decreasing fraction width often improve range but worsen local precision? Use one formula and one numeric comparison from the workbook. Model explanation The exponent selects the scale 2^(E−β), while m fraction bits determine the local step 2^(k−m). With the same 16-bit total, BF16 allocates more exponent bits than FP16 but only 7 fraction bits instead of 10. At [1,2), BF16 spacing is 1/128 and FP16 spacing is 1/1024, an eightfold difference. This explains the source’s range/precision comparison without asserting a measured accuracy result. Self-review rubric For encoding/decoding, award yourself one check each for field boundaries, representation branch, bias/scale, fraction arithmetic, and reverse verification. For conceptual answers, require a mechanism, the stated assumption, and a consequence. For quantization extensions, also require a rounding policy and a clipping check. A final number with the wrong branch is not a correct solution. What this does not show The mathematical examples do not specify quantizer training, calibration algorithms, per-channel scaling, integer matrix-multiply implementation, accumulator overflow behavior, or task accuracy from the review’s one-page quantization definition. Its exact bit patterns concern the stated source formats; especially for very low-bit formats, field widths alone do not determine infinity/NaN rules or exponent bias. Runtime handling of subnormals is also outside these source examples. Use the main midterm worked guide for layer shapes, parameter/MAC/activation counts, pruning criteria, and automatic pruning methods. For Lecture 7, the mathematical goal is: know which branch of a numeric format you are reading, reconstruct its real value, and state what error that representation can introduce. Go deeper in the supplied material First reread signed integer conventions ; then practice the FP32 encoding and FP16 decoding . After those calculations are fluent, test your understanding with the low-bit codebook comparison and the constructed affine exercises above. Read the instructor’s 98-page review ↗ ★ Source-star priorities are shown by topic. All 98 pages were visually checked; 42 pages have actual yellow stars. Practice panels contain answers: attempt the prompt before expanding. No external scripts, fonts, or network assets are required. Find a question family 1. Quantization maps a continuous choice onto a discrete set 15. Use the concept map to choose your explanation 1. Read the problem as a resource-accounting contract Source pages 2–23 This guide explains the mathematical and conceptual question families in the supplied Mid-term Review.pdf . A yellow star in the actual PDF is a priority marker; the stars here identify those source topics, including repeated slides. The review has 98 pages and 42 genuinely starred pages. Five explicit example questions occupy pages 3–23. Their intent is to test whether you can connect the shape of a computation to its storage, activation memory, arithmetic, or pruning behavior. The PDF says the exam covers Lectures 1–7 and uses multiple-choice, conceptual, and short-answer questions; it also describes separate undergraduate and graduate papers and a handwritten single-sided letter-size cheat sheet. These are source statements, not a prediction of the questions you will receive. [Review PDF pp. 2] Every new exercise in this guide uses constructed inputs . These exercises preserve the review's operations and reasoning difficulty while changing dimensions, values, or the context. The solutions expose each step rather than giving a number without a method. Exact counts are exact integers; decimal floating-point boundary values are approximations where marked. No graph is treated as a hidden numerical table. Read the contract shape, units, bias, batch Choose a formula what is being counted? Check assumptions groups, padding, live buffers Explain the result and its practical limit A correct calculation begins with the quantities the prompt actually asks for. Use a three-column scratch table: given , formula , and answer with units . Parameter count means learned constants, activation count means runtime tensor elements, MAC count means multiply-accumulate operations, and measured latency means elapsed time on a specified system. A formula for one cannot silently replace another. Notation throughout: B is batch size; Cᵢ and Cₒ are input/output channels or features; H,W are spatial sizes; K is kernel size; S is stride; P is symmetric padding; G is group count. Parameters and MACs ignore bias unless stated. Tensor layouts are written in the order shown by the course, without assuming every software library stores tensors in that order. 2. ★ Dense layers connect every output to every input Source pages 3–5; 30; 32; 44; 56 A fully connected layer makes each output feature a weighted sum of all input features. If input X has shape (B,Cᵢ), then W has shape (Cₒ,Cᵢ), bias b has shape (Cₒ), and output Y has shape (B,Cₒ). With rows of X representing examples, the computation is Y=XWᵀ+b, where the bias is broadcast across rows. [Review PDF pp. 3–5, 32] y j = Σ i=1…Cᵢ w ji x i + b j Why does W have this shape? One output requires Cᵢ coefficients. There are Cₒ outputs, so there are Cₒ rows of Cᵢ coefficients. This gives CᵢCₒ weights and, when enabled, Cₒ biases. The weights are shared by all B examples; increasing the batch increases output elements and arithmetic, not the number of distinct learned constants. Weights = CᵢCₒ; parameters with bias = CᵢCₒ+Cₒ; activations = BCₒ; MACs = BCᵢCₒ The network diagram distinguishes depth , the number of successive layers, from width , the number of hidden features or neurons in a layer. Increasing width changes a layer’s feature dimensions and often increases parameters; increasing batch changes how many examples use those layers. These are separate axes of model shape. [Review PDF p. 30] Source Example Question 1, fully explained The input shape is (4,2), and there are 6 output neurons. Step 1: Cᵢ=2 and Cₒ=6. Step 2: W has shape (6,2), so the weights number 6×2=12. Step 3: each output has one bias, giving 6 more learned values. Therefore trainable parameters are 12+6= 18 . The output shape is (4,6). The last output-shape observation is an explanatory extension to the two questions asked on the slide. The source answer agrees. [Review PDF pp. 3–5] A common wrong answer multiplies 18 by the batch size. That would imply four independent models. A batch applies the same model to four inputs, so 18 parameters remain 18 parameters. Practice D1: Constructed: input (3,5), dense layer with 7 outputs and bias. Find weight shape, parameter count, output shape, and MACs. W=(7,5). Its 35 coefficients plus 7 biases give 42 parameters . Output is (3,7), so there are 21 output activations. For arithmetic, each of 3×7 outputs takes 5 MACs: 3×7×5= 105 MACs . Bias additions are excluded from this MAC convention. Parameters and arithmetic have different batch dependence. Practice D2: Constructed: input (2,9), dense layer with 4 outputs and bias. Which result changes if batch becomes 8? W=(4,9), weights=36, parameters=36+4= 40 , output=(2,4), and MACs=2×4×9= 72 . Changing B to 8 leaves W and the 40 parameters fixed but multiplies the activation count and MAC count by 4. The original output has 8 elements; the new output has 32. Short-answer self-check: your explanation should name both feature dimensions, show the separate weight and bias terms, and explicitly state that batch does not change learned parameter count. 3. ★ Convolution counts local connections repeated across space Source pages 33–35; 44–47; 56–57 A convolution filter sees a local receptive field rather than the whole input image. A standard 2D convolution has W shape (Cₒ,Cᵢ,Kₕ,K𝑤); each output channel has its own kernel, and the kernel is reused at every output position. Reuse is why parameter count is independent of image resolution even while arithmetic and activations grow with resolution. [Review PDF pp. 33–34, 45] Hₒ = ⌊(Hᵢ+2Pₕ−Kₕ)/Sₕ⌋+1; Wₒ = ⌊(Wᵢ+2P𝑤−K𝑤)/S𝑤⌋+1 These shape formulas assume dilation 1, symmetric padding, and ordinary floor-based output sizing. If a problem changes dilation or uses a different padding convention, read that explicitly. The floor matters: with a stride greater than one, you cannot casually cancel terms and promise that doubling an input will double every output dimension exactly. Weights = CₒCᵢKₕK𝑤; output activations = BCₒHₒWₒ; MACs = BCₒHₒWₒCᵢKₕK𝑤 Derivation: one output value is the dot product of CᵢKₕK𝑤 input/kernel pairs. There are BCₒHₒWₒ outputs. Multiply those two counts. The same weights participate repeatedly, so multiplying weight count by B or output area would confuse how often a weight is used with how many weights exist. Practice C1: Constructed: B=1, input 4×16×16, 8 output channels, 3×3 kernel, stride 2, padding 1. Find shape, weights, and MACs. Hₒ=Wₒ=⌊(16+2−3)/2⌋+1=⌊15/2⌋+1=8. Output is 8×8×8 . Weights=8×4×3×3= 288 . Output activations=8×8×8= 512 . Each activation needs 4×3×3=36 MACs, so MACs=512×36= 18,432 . With bias, parameters would be 288+8=296; the requested weights-only answer remains 288. Practice C2: Constructed: B=1, input 3×15×15, 6 output channels, 5×5 kernel, stride 1, no padding. Find output and resource counts. Hₒ=Wₒ=15−5+1=11. Output is 6×11×11 . Weights=6×3×25= 450 . Activations=6×121= 726 . MACs=726×75= 54,450 . No padding reduces spatial size; using 15×15 in the MAC formula would overcount outputs. The starred 1D convolution uses the same reasoning on one spatial axis For 1D convolution, input X has shape (B,Cᵢ,Wᵢ), output Y has shape (B,Cₒ,Wₒ), weights W have shape (Cₒ,Cᵢ,K), and bias has shape (Cₒ). Each output sees CᵢK inputs. With dilation 1, Wₒ=⌊(Wᵢ+2P−K)/S⌋+1; weights=CₒCᵢK; output activations=BCₒWₒ; MACs=BCₒWₒCᵢK. The 2D formulas add a second spatial kernel/output dimension rather than introducing a different counting principle. [Review PDF p. 33] Grouped and depthwise convolutions require a different input-channel factor With G groups, each output sees Cᵢ/G input channels. Assume G divides both channel counts. The formulas become weights=Cₒ(Cᵢ/G)KₕK𝑤 and MACs=BCₒHₒWₒ(Cᵢ/G)KₕK𝑤. Output activation count stays BCₒHₒWₒ. The review lists group and depthwise formulas alongside dense convolution. [Review PDF pp. 45, 57] Depthwise convolution with one output per input channel has G=Cᵢ=Cₒ; weights=CᵢKₕK𝑤 and MACs=BCᵢHₒWₒKₕK𝑤. A subsequent pointwise 1×1 convolution has its own weights and MACs; it is not included just because the word “depthwise” appears. Practice G1: Constructed: 8 input channels, 12 outputs, G=4, 3×3 kernel, output 10×10, B=1. Compare grouped and standard weights. Each output sees 8/4=2 input channels. Grouped weights=12×2×9= 216 ; activations=12×100=1,200; MACs=1,200×18= 21,600 . Standard convolution would have 12×8×9=864 weights and 86,400 MACs, four times as many. A separate depthwise layer with 8 input/output channels and the same 10×10 output uses 8×9= 72 weights and 7,200 MACs . Practice G2: Constructed: 12 inputs, 16 outputs, G=4, 3×3 kernel, output 8×8, B=1. Also count a separate 12-channel depthwise layer. Grouped weights=16×(12/4)×9= 432 ; activations=16×64=1,024; MACs=1,024×27= 27,648 . For the separate depthwise layer, weights=12×9= 108 ; MACs=12×64×9= 6,912 . Do not compare layers as interchangeable architectures: their connectivity and output channels differ. Pooling changes shape without learned weights Max pooling selects the largest local input; average pooling computes a local average. The review shows channelwise pooling with kernel size equal to stride and no learnable parameters. A 2×2, stride-2 pool on an even-sized map halves H and W and preserves C. Its output still contains activations. In the review's MAC accounting table max pooling has zero MACs; that does not mean it takes zero comparisons or zero runtime. [Review PDF pp. 23, 35] Nonlinear activations such as ReLU act after weighted sums. ReLU is max(0,x); ReLU6 additionally caps the value at 6. These functions are why stacking neural layers can express more than one linear transformation. For an ordinary ReLU on values [−2,0,3], the outputs are [0,0,3]; this is an explanatory microexample, not an additional architecture count. [Review PDF pp. 36] 4. ★ Activation memory depends on area and on what remains live Source pages 6–8; 19–20; 51–53 The second source example asks why CNN memory is uneven across depth, and what doubling input resolution changes. Early layers usually retain large H×W maps, creating many activation elements. Later layers downsample their maps; more channels do not necessarily offset the reduced spatial area. Parameters can become a larger fraction of layer memory later. This is a tendency illustrated by the review's CNN plots, not a theorem that every CNN follows. [Review PDF pp. 6–8, 53] Activation elements = BC×H×W; activation bytes = BC×H×W×(bits per activation)/8 If both H and W scale by a factor a while B and C are fixed, activation count scales by a². This explains the source's roughly fourfold increase when each image dimension doubles. Convolution kernel dimensions and channel counts do not change, so first-layer parameter count is unchanged. The “roughly” qualification matters when stride and rounding prevent exact doubling of output dimensions. Practice M1: Constructed: a stride-1 same-size convolution produces 8×32×32. Input dimensions double; channels stay fixed. What changes? Original outputs=8×32×32= 8,192 . New outputs=8×64×64= 32,768 . Ratio=32,768/8,192= 4 . Weights do not change because Cᵢ,Cₒ and the kernel are fixed. MACs also increase fourfold because the kernel is applied at four times as many output positions. Practice M2: Constructed: output 12×24×24 becomes 12×36×36, same convolution filter bank. Find count and ratio. Original activations=12×24²= 6,912 . New activations=12×36²= 15,552 . Ratio=(36/24)²= 2.25 . A 50% increase in each dimension means a 125% increase in area, not a 50% increase. The number of weights remains constant. Total activation count is not peak activation memory The review's AlexNet slide reports 932,264 total activation elements, including its 150,528 input elements. Output tensors alone sum to 781,736 . Its simplified peak is input plus first-convolution output: 150,528+290,400= 440,928 . This convention counts the input as part of the total and uses adjacent live input/output buffers for the peak. It is an approximation to runtime memory, not a full allocator trace. [Review PDF pp. 20, 52] To estimate a chain's peak under that convention, evaluate Aᵢ₋₁+Aᵢ for each operation, then take the maximum. Multiply by bytes per element. A runtime may reuse buffers, keep skip connections alive, allocate convolution workspaces, or keep training intermediates. Those effects can change the actual peak without changing the mathematical output tensor shapes. Practice M3: Constructed: input 3×16×16 and output 8×16×16 coexist, FP32 activations. Estimate this operation's live activation bytes. Input count=3×256=768; output count=8×256=2,048. Live count=768+2,048= 2,816 . FP32 uses 4 bytes per element, so live bytes=2,816×4= 11,264 bytes . This answer is for the specified two tensors and does not include weights or workspace. Practice M4: Constructed: input 8×16×16 and output 16×8×8 coexist, FP16 activations. Estimate bytes. Counts are 8×256=2,048 and 16×64=1,024. Live count= 3,072 . FP16 uses 2 bytes each, giving 6,144 bytes . Although channels doubled, output activation count halved because spatial area fell by a factor of four. Conceptual variant: why can a model with fewer parameters still run out of activation memory? Explainer: parameter count measures learned weight elements; activation count depends on batch, resolution, and feature maps. Keeping large early maps or several live branches can dominate memory even when the model's weight file is small. Name the relevant tensors instead of assuming that a smaller file guarantees a smaller working set. 5. ★ A layer-by-layer table makes whole-network questions manageable Source pages 16–18; 23; 46–47 The original Example Question 5 on PDF page 16 visibly presents three layers : a 3→16, 3×3 stride-1 pad-1 convolution; a 2×2 stride-2 max pool; and a 16→32, 3×3 stride-1 pad-1 convolution. The input is 3×512×512, batch 1. Page 23 gives these three rows. A larger seven-layer architecture is shown separately on pages 18 and 47. We keep the original question and that extension separate. [Review PDF pp. 16, 18, 23, 47] Start with shape propagation. For the first convolution Hₒ=512+2−3+1=512. Pooling halves 512 to 256. The second padded stride-1 convolution preserves 256. Next compute weights, output elements, and MACs independently for each row. This avoids carrying one mistaken interpretation through all three columns. Source Q5 layer Output Weights only Output elements MACs Conv1, 3→16 16×512×512 432 4,194,304 113,246,208 MaxPool 16×256×256 0 1,048,576 0 Conv2, 16→32 32×256×256 4,608 2,097,152 301,989,888 The first row follows from weights=16×3×9=432, activations=16×512²=4,194,304, and MACs=4,194,304×27=113,246,208. The third row follows from weights=32×16×9=4,608, activations=32×256²=2,097,152, and MACs=2,097,152×144=301,989,888. Pooling has outputs but no trainable weights or MACs under this convention. [Review PDF pp. 90–94] Smallest subnormal = 2 1−β−m ; largest subnormal = (1−2 −m )2 1−β Smallest normal = 2 1−β ; largest finite = (2−2 −m )2 (2ᵉ−2)−β Practice B1: Constructed exam variant: derive the four positive FP16 boundaries using e=5,m=10,β=15. Minimum subnormal=2¹⁻¹⁵⁻¹⁰= 2⁻²⁴≈5.960464478×10⁻⁸ . Maximum subnormal=(1−2⁻¹⁰)2⁻¹⁴= ≈6.097555161×10⁻⁵ . Minimum normal=2⁻¹⁴= ≈6.103515625×10⁻⁵ . Maximum finite=(2−2⁻¹⁰)2¹⁵= 65,504 . The max-subnormal/min-normal gap is exactly one subnormal step, 2⁻²⁴. Practice B2: Constructed exam variant: derive the FP32 largest subnormal and minimum normal using m=23,β=127. Largest subnormal= (1−2⁻²³)2⁻¹²⁶≈1.175494211×10⁻³⁸ ; minimum normal= 2⁻¹²⁶≈1.175494351×10⁻³⁸ . Their difference is 2⁻¹⁴⁹, the smallest positive subnormal. Filling fraction bits approaches the smallest normal from below but does not equal it. For normal numbers in the interval [2ᵏ,2ᵏ⁺¹), one fraction-bit unit changes x by 2ᵏ⁻ᵐ. Exponent width primarily controls representable range; fraction width primarily controls local precision. More bits in one field do not automatically improve the other. FP32 and BF16 both have eight exponent bits, while FP32's larger fraction field resolves much smaller relative differences. The review compares FP32, FP16, BF16, and FP8 layouts. [Review PDF pp. 94, 96] Practice PRES1: Constructed: FP16 spacing near 1 versus near 8, m=10. Compute. Near 1, k=0 and spacing=2⁰⁻¹⁰= 2⁻¹⁰=0.0009765625 . Near 8, k=3 and spacing=2³⁻¹⁰= 2⁻⁷=0.0078125 . The absolute spacing is eight times larger, while the precision relative to scale is similar. At a power-of-two boundary, spacing differs immediately below and above the boundary. Practice PRES2: Constructed: a binary normal format has m=7. What is spacing near 1, and how does FP16 compare there? Spacing near 1 is 2⁻⁷= 0.0078125 . FP16 has m=10 and spacing 2⁻¹⁰, so it has eight times finer spacing near 1. This calculation compares local resolution only; exponent width and special-value rules are needed to compare range. The source's FP4 value sets are toy conventions, not IEEE contracts Page 97 illustrates INT4 and three four-bit floating layouts: E1M2, E2M1, and E3M0. Some diagram labels and annotated bit-pattern equations disagree, and some layouts use all exponents as finite values rather than reserving IEEE special cases. For instance, its E2M1 top pattern is annotated with a formula (1+0.5)×2³⁻¹, which evaluates to 6 , although a nearby printed result says 1. The displayed E2M1 value list includes 6. Do not learn the inconsistent label as arithmetic. [Review PDF pp. 97] For the following questions, the displayed positive value sets are the supplied contract: E1M2 uses [0,0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,3.5]; E2M1 uses [0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6]; E3M0 uses [0,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8,16]. These sets illustrate dense local coverage versus broader range. Their rules must not be inferred solely from the phrase “floating point.” Practice TINY1: Constructed: round 2.7 to the nearest E2M1 value from [0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6]. Compare with E1M2's supplied set. E2M1: distances to 2 and 3 are 0.7 and 0.3, so choose 3 . E1M2 additionally has 2.5, at distance 0.2, so choose 2.5 . The format with the larger range need not have the smaller error for this input. Practice TINY2: Constructed: round 0.6 to the nearest E3M0 value from [0,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8,16]. Explain the tradeoff. The nearest is 0.5 because its distance is 0.1, smaller than the distance to 1 or 0.25. E3M0 reaches 16 but has widely separated large values. More exponent allocation gives range at the expense of mantissa resolution. Here the exercise uses an explicit value list, avoiding ambiguous bit-pattern rules. 14. Quantization maps a continuous choice onto a discrete set Source pages 98; extension The last review page defines quantization as restricting values from a continuous or large set to a discrete set. Its examples connect continuous signals to quantized levels and images to reduced colors. A quantized value introduces quantization error: the difference between the original and reconstructed values. The slide does not supply an affine scale/zero-point formula or a full quantization algorithm. The simple numerical rule below is therefore a clearly labeled explanatory extension , useful for practicing the definition without attributing an unsupplied formula to the Lecture 7 slides. [Review PDF pp. 98] Extension: q = clip(round(x/s),q min ,q max ); reconstructed x̂=sq; error=|x−x̂| Assume positive scale s, integer output q, zero point 0, nearest rounding, and the specified integer bounds. No example below is an exact halfway tie, so tie-breaking does not affect these answers. Without clipping, nearest rounding error is at most s/2. Clipping can create a larger error for inputs outside representable range. Practice Q1: Constructed extension: s=0.25, signed integer bounds [−8,7], x=0.62. Quantize and reconstruct. x/s=0.62/0.25=2.48. Nearest integer= q=2 ; it is inside bounds. Reconstruct x̂=2×0.25= 0.5 . Absolute error=|0.62−0.5|= 0.12 , below s/2=0.125. Practice Q2: Constructed extension: s=0.2, bounds [−8,7], x=−0.88. Quantize and reconstruct. x/s=−4.4, so nearest integer= q=−4 . Reconstructed value= −0.8 ; error= 0.08 . Negative inputs round by closeness on the number line; taking absolute value first would discard the sign. Practice Q3: Constructed extension: s=0.25, bounds [−8,7], x=2.0. Why does the half-step error bound fail? x/s=8; rounding gives 8 but the allowed maximum is 7. Clip to q=7 and reconstruct 1.75 . Error= 0.25 , larger than 0.125. The half-step bound assumed the input lies in the covered range without clipping. Conceptual variant: is the fourfold weight-storage saving of moving FP32 to INT8 enough to show unchanged quality? Explainer: no. Storage is determined by count and width, while quality depends on how the mapping changes computations and on calibration or training. Check error and task accuracy. The course's efficiency-accuracy tradeoff still applies. searchText: From a sliding kernel to an exam answer The worked explanations and practice solutions work without JavaScript. Enable JavaScript to use the eight interactive labs. Efficient AI · An intuitive exam companion From a sliding kernel to an exam answer A convolution is a small calculation repeated in many places. Start with four multiplications you can see, then learn how shape tells you how many times to repeat them. Each formula below comes with its meaning, a worked example, and a way to test your understanding. Open the instructor’s midterm review ↗ Read this in order if the formulas feel unfamiliar. The first half builds convolution from ordinary multiplication and addition; the second explains every yellow-star concept family in the 98-page review. Toy numbers and labs are constructed teaching examples. Stars label source priorities, not predictions of exam questions. 1. Understand the objects 2. Slide and calculate 3. Derive shape 4. Add channels 5. Count the work 6. Solve a network 7. Review the stars 8. Practise an exam calculation Input numbers What arrives Weights + rule What is reused Output numbers What is computed Count & explain What the exam asks Shape counts the slots. Arithmetic fills the slots. Parameters describe the reusable rule. 1 · A shape is a labelled address system for numbers A scalar is one number, such as 7. A vector is a row or list of numbers. A matrix is a rectangular grid. A tensor is the general name for an array with any number of axes. You already understand the essential idea: a spreadsheet has rows and columns; a batch of colour images needs more labels. A tensor’s shape lists how many slots there are along each axis. Shape tells you where a number can be stored, not what the number’s value is. [Review pp. 32–35] A 2×3 matrix has two rows and three columns: six stored numbers. Its shape is (2,3). Multiplying 2×3 counts slots; it does not multiply the six values inside the matrix. This distinction is the reason a convolution question can ask for both the output values and the number of output elements . Term or symbol Plain meaning What to ask yourself N, also n or B Batch size: number of independent images processed together How many examples share the same model? C in , also c i Input channels: grids describing one image How many grids arrive per image? H in , W in Input height and width: rows and columns of each grid How large is each arriving grid? C out , also c o Output channels: number of complete filters and resulting maps How many different filters are applied? K h , K w Kernel height and width: size of each local weight slice How many neighbouring positions does it inspect? S, P, D, G Stride, padding, dilation, groups; explained step by step below Where can it move, and which channels connect? The review uses NCHW order: (batch, channels, height, width). The example (2,3,4,5) means two images, each containing three grids, each grid four rows high and five columns wide. It stores 2×3×4×5=120 numbers. For one image, CHW=(3,4,5) stores 60. RGB is a familiar three-channel input: separate red, green, and blue values at each pixel. Later channels are calculated feature responses, not necessarily colours or recognisable objects. A feature map is one spatial grid of such responses; its entries are activations . [Review p. 34] Some software writes NHWC=(2,4,5,3). That changes the order of the labels, not the total 120 entries. Never read the first number as channels until the axis order is given. Also, batch size is not network width: increasing N repeats the same model on more examples. Try: what does (4,2,3,5) mean, and how many numbers does it contain? N=4 images; C=2 grids per image; H=3 rows; W=5 columns. One grid has 3×5=15 entries. One image has 2×15=30 entries. The batch has 4×30= 120 entries . The equality with the earlier example’s count does not make the shapes interchangeable. 2 · A kernel makes one output by multiplying a patch and adding A weight is a coefficient in a calculation. A kernel , in the spatial sense used here, is a small grid of weights. A patch is the matching small region of input values under that grid. Place the kernel over the patch, multiply corresponding positions, then add the products. This repeated local calculation is what a CNN calls convolution. We use the deep-learning cross-correlation convention: the kernel is not flipped. Mathematical convolution can use a flipped kernel, so follow the convention stated by the problem. [Review pp. 33–34] [Conv2d, operator] Take patch [[1,2],[5,6]] and kernel [[1,2],[0,−1]]. Read matching positions in the same order. Top left: 1×1=1. Top right: 2×2=4. Bottom left: 5×0=0. Bottom right: 6×(−1)=−6. Add: 1+4+0−6= −1 . The result is one scalar, not a 2×2 output. Four input values collapse into one response. That calculation is a dot product : pair matching entries, multiply, and add. The symbol Σ means “add all the terms described after me.” Writing Σx i w i is shorthand for x 1 w 1 +x 2 w 2 +…; it is not an extra mysterious operation. An index such as i tells you which entry to use. A bias is a learned offset added after the sum. Bias 2 would change −1 to 1. Now move the same weights one column right. The new patch is [[2,3],[6,7]]. The sum becomes 2×1+3×2+6×0+7×(−1)=2+6+0−7= 1 . The weights were reused; only the input patch changed. Continue to build the whole output grid. Kernels can learn useful local patterns, but these hand-chosen weights are teaching examples, not a trained edge detector. Lab 1 · Move the kernel and see every product Edit an input or weight. Select an output cell to see its highlighted input patch. Coordinates start at row 0, column 0. Grey cells are zero padding. Stride S 1 2 Padding P 0 1 Bias Input, with the current patch Reusable 2×2 weights Output: choose a position Previous position Next position Reset example Predict first: with S=1 and P=0, why do four rows of input produce only three rows of output? Use the next section to explain it. Try: patch [[2,−1],[3,4]], kernel [[1,2],[−1,0]], bias 3. Find one output. Pair corresponding entries: 2×1, (−1)×2, 3×(−1), 4×0. Products are 2, −2, −3, 0. Sum the products: 2−2−3+0=−3. Add bias once: −3+3= 0 . Do not add the bias once for every product. 3 · Output shape counts the places where the window fits Stride is the distance between successive window anchors. Stride 1 moves one position at a time; stride 2 moves two. Padding adds a border, usually zeros, so a kernel can inspect boundary regions. Padding P=1 adds one row above and below and one column on each side. It adds two to each spatial size, not one, and not two times the entire image area. Derive the row count before memorising the formula. A length-4 input and length-2 kernel have valid starting rows 0,1,2: three positions. The last start is 4−2=2. With stride 1, the starts are 0 through 2, giving (4−2)/1+1=3. The +1 counts the first start at 0. With stride 2, the starts are 0 and 2, giving (4−2)/2+1=2. If the last start is not exactly reachable, you round down: you cannot place half a window. H out = floor((H in + 2P h − K h )/S h ) + 1 W out = floor((W in + 2P w − K w )/S w ) + 1 floor means the largest integer no greater than the value: floor(3.5)=3. This formula assumes dilation 1 and equal padding on opposite sides. A kernel dimension must fit inside the padded input; otherwise this is invalid geometry, not a tensor with a negative number of rows. Compute height and width separately when they differ. [Review pp. 18, 34, 47] Worked rectangular example, constructed. Input H=5, W=7; K=3×3; S=2; P=1. Height: floor((5+2−3)/2)+1=floor(4/2)+1=3. Width: floor((7+2−3)/2)+1=floor(6/2)+1=4. The output has 3×4=12 positions per map. It is not square merely because the kernel is square. With four filters it becomes C×H×W=4×3×4; with batch 2, NCHW=(2,4,3,4). Why the floor matters. H=8, K=3, P=0, S=2 gives floor(5/2)+1=3. The valid anchors are 0,2,4. An anchor at 6 would need rows 6,7,8, but the final input row is 7. It cannot fit. Rounding 2.5 upward would invent an invalid fourth window. Dilation, optional extension. Dilation D spaces the kernel’s taps apart. A three-tap kernel with D=2 touches offsets 0,2,4: it spans five positions while still containing three weights. Replace K by the effective kernel size K eff =D(K−1)+1. A 3×3 kernel at D=2 spans 5×5 positions but still has nine coefficients per channel slice. The calculator includes this extension; the basic review examples use D=1. [Conv2d, dilation and Shape] Lab 2 · Read the formula as an explanation Use “Apply dimensions” after editing. G=1 is ordinary convolution; grouped and depthwise connectivity are explained below. Counts include the chosen batch; weights are counted only once. Include one bias per output channel Apply dimensions RGB example Depthwise example Try: input (1,2,9,11), 3 filters, 3×3 kernel, stride 2, padding 0. Find the output shape. Keep batch N=1. Set output channels to the three filters: C out =3. Height: floor((9−3)/2)+1=4. Width: floor((11−3)/2)+1=5. Output NCHW= (1,3,4,5) ; 1×3×4×5= 60 entries . You do not need the actual pixel values to answer a shape question. 4 · One filter adds contributions from all its input channels So far the input had one channel. An ordinary convolutional filter for an RGB image contains three spatial kernel slices: one for red, one for green, one for blue. It computes three local dot products at a position and adds them, then adds one bias. Those partial sums become one output entry. They do not become three separate output maps. A complete filter sees the whole input depth. [Review p. 34] Input channel 1 patch × slice 1 contribution 0 Input channel 2 patch × slice 2 contribution 5 Add 0 + 5 + bias 2 one output value: 7 Repeat over positions Two channels feed one filter. Making three complete filters gives three output maps, not six. Constructed two-channel example: channel 1 patch [[1,2],[0,1]], slice 1 [[1,0],[1,−1]] gives 1+0+0−1=0. Channel 2 patch [[3,0],[2,1]], slice 2 [[0,1],[2,1]] gives 0+0+4+1=5. Add both contributions and bias 2: 0+5+2=7. A different complete filter could use different slices and yield a different response at the same position. Here is the general sum translated into actions, with one image index n, output-filter index o, and output position (r,c): Y[n,o,r,c] = b[o] + Σ input channels i Σ kernel rows u Σ kernel columns v W[o,i,u,v] · X padded [n,i,rS h +uD h ,cS w +vD w ] Choose one image n and one complete filter o. Choose the output row r and column c. Multiply by stride to get the input window’s starting position. For each input channel i, visit each kernel row u and column v. Dilation spaces those visits apart. Multiply each input value by its matching weight; add every product from every connected channel. Add the filter’s bias once. Put that one result into Y[n,o,r,c]. For ordinary convolution, the weight tensor is (C out ,C in ,K h ,K w ) . Four filters, three input channels, 3×3 slices means (4,3,3,3): 12 spatial slices and 108 weights, producing four maps. Neither batch nor image height appears in that weight shape. [Review p. 34] Lab 3 · Add channel contributions into one output Keep the first slice fixed. Multiply all four weights in the second slice by a gain, then add the bias. The input still has two channels when gain=0; zero weights alone do not rebuild a smaller layer. Second-slice gain Bias Groups change the connections. With G groups, each output filter sees C in /G input channels. Both C in and C out must be divisible by G. For C in =4, C out =6, G=2, each filter sees two channels; there are three output filters in each group. Its 3×3 weight count is 6×2×9=108, half the ungrouped 6×4×9=216. Depthwise convolution in the review’s basic case uses G=C in =C out : one spatial slice per channel. Eight channels with 3×3 slices need 8×9=72 weights. A following 1×1 pointwise convolution mixes channels; count it separately if present. [Review, parameter/MAC tables] [Conv2d, groups] 5 · Parameters count the rule; activations count answers; MACs count repeated work A parameter is a learned value stored in the model. In these resource formulas, “weights only” excludes biases. A MAC , multiply–accumulate, means multiplying an input by a weight and adding it to a running sum. Counting MACs is a convention for the main dot-product work; it need not exactly equal the number of separate additions in a hand-written sum. The review counts one MAC per weighted term and omits bias addition and pooling comparisons. [Review pp. 21–23, 55–60] Question Formula for a grouped 2D conv Meaning of each factor Weights only C out ×(C in /G)×K h ×K w Filters × channels seen per filter × weights per slice Weights + bias Weights + C out One learned offset per complete filter Output activations N×C out ×H out ×W out Images × maps × rows × columns MACs Output activations × (C in /G)×K h ×K w Answers × weighted terms needed for each answer Apply the rectangular example from section 3: N=2, C in =3, C out =4, output 3×4, K=3×3, G=1. One filter needs 3×9=27 coefficients. Four filters need 4×27= 108 weights ; with biases, 108+4= 112 parameters . Outputs: 2 images×4 maps×3 rows×4 columns= 96 activations . Each activation needs 27 weighted terms, so 96×27= 2,592 MACs . This order makes the MAC formula understandable: count how many answers, then count the work per answer. Larger spatial maps reuse the weights more times; they do not create new weights. Doubling H and W approximately quadruples output activations and MACs when other settings stay fixed. Exact stride/padding floors can change that ratio. The parameters stay the same. Doubling batch N doubles activations and MACs, also without changing parameters. Doubling filters doubles parameters, output activations, and MACs. These are different edits, even when some totals change by the same factor. To change counts into storage, specify a bit width q. Bytes=number of entries×q/8 if entries are densely packed and metadata is ignored. The 112-parameter example in FP32 (32 bits=4 bytes) occupies 112×4=448 bytes of parameter data. Its 96 outputs occupy 384 bytes. Those are different memory objects; actual inference also needs live inputs and possibly temporary workspaces. FLOPs count floating-point arithmetic work. Under the review’s two-operations-per-MAC convention, 2,592 MACs correspond to 5,184 FLOPs. FLOPS , with S meaning “per second,” is a rate. Dividing 5,184 FLOPs by a hypothetical sustained 1,000,000 FLOPs/s gives 0.005184 seconds=5.184 milliseconds of arithmetic time under that assumption. It is not measured latency: data movement and execution overhead also matter. [Review pp. 38–61] Try: N=3, input channels 2, output channels 5, output map 4×6, 3×3 kernel, G=1. Count weights, bias-inclusive parameters, outputs, MACs. Weights per filter=2×3×3=18. Five filters: 90 weights . Add five biases: 95 parameters . Output entries=3×5×4×6= 360 . Work per output=18 MACs. Total=360×18= 6,480 MACs . At two FLOPs/MAC: 12,960 FLOPs . 6 · A dense layer uses the same dot-product idea without sliding A dense or fully connected layer connects every input feature to every output neuron. A feature here is one number per example. If one example has three features and you want two outputs, create two rows of three weights. Each output row does one dot product with the same input vector. Convolution shares a local rule across positions; a dense layer operates on the full input vector. [Review pp. 3–5, 32] Constructed example: x=[2,−1,3]. Weight row 1=[1,0,2], bias 1; row 2=[−1,3,1], bias 0. Output 1 is 2×1+(−1)×0+3×2+1=9. Output 2 is 2×(−1)+(−1)×3+3×1+0=−2. The output is [9,−2]. There are six weights, two biases, eight learned parameters, two output values, and six MACs for one example. For N examples with C in features and C out neurons: input X has shape (N,C in ); weights W have shape (C out ,C in ); bias b has shape (C out ); output Y has shape (N,C out ). Matrix notation writes Y=XW T +b . The superscript T means transpose: swap W’s row and column axes so the matrix dimensions match. The bias vector is reused for every example, an operation called broadcasting. The review’s actual Q1 gives N=4, C in =2, C out =6. W=(6,2); weights=6×2=12; plus six biases gives 18 parameters . The 4 is a batch count, so it is not multiplied into 18. If additionally asked, Y=(4,6), activations=24, MACs=4×6×2=48. [Review pp. 3–5] Lab 4 · Watch two dense neurons use the same features x₁ x₂ x₃ Fixed weight rows: [1,0,2] and [−1,3,1]. Fixed biases: 1 and 0. Matrix-multiplication exam rule. An (m,k) matrix multiplied by a (k,n) matrix produces (m,n). The shared inner dimension k counts the weighted terms per output. There are m×n outputs, each with k MACs, giving m×n×k MACs . Example: (2,3)×(3,4) gives (2,4), eight outputs, three terms each, 24 MACs. It cannot be multiplied if the two inner dimensions differ. [Review pp. 21, 55] 7 · Pooling chooses or averages numbers inside each channel A pooling window reduces spatial resolution with a fixed rule. Max pooling returns the largest number in a patch; average pooling returns its arithmetic mean. Neither uses a learned kernel of coefficients in the ordinary pooling layer. Pooling runs separately on every channel: it does not combine RGB into one channel. Its output batch and channel counts are unchanged. Use the same window-fitting reasoning to find H out and W out ; the basic examples use padding 0. [Review p. 35] On [[1,2],[5,6]], max is 6; average is (1+2+5+6)/4=14/4=3.5. A 4×4 map pooled with a 2×2 window and stride 2 becomes 2×2. For input (2,4,8,10), that pooling produces (2,4,4,5): output elements=160, learned parameters=0. Under the review’s weighted-MAC accounting, max-pool MACs=0; finding a maximum still requires comparisons. “Zero parameters” and “zero MACs” do not mean “zero execution time.” An activation function changes each value using a rule. ReLU(x)=max(0,x) keeps positive values and replaces negative values with zero. It normally keeps tensor shape unchanged. Pooling instead changes spatial size. Convolution, ReLU, and pooling are three different stages; never add the pooling window size to the convolution parameter count. Lab 5 · Compare max, average, and ReLU Fixed constructed input is shown below. Every output uses a non-overlapping 2×2 patch. Toggle ReLU to replace negative inputs with zero before pooling. In binary, the columns are powers of two: …, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Each column contains either 0 or 1. So binary 1010 is 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 0 × 1 = 10 . The notation 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8; the superscript is an exponent, the number of repeated factors. Negative powers describe fractions: 2⁻¹ = 1/2; 2⁻² = 1/4; 2⁻³ = 1/8. Binary 0.101 therefore means 1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8 = 0.625 . These are the same place values that will appear in a floating-point fraction. E1M2 allocates 1 exponent and 2 fraction bits after the sign: its nonnegative values are 0,0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,3.5. E3M0 allocates 3 exponent and no fraction bits: 0,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8,16. It reaches farther but leaves larger gaps at high magnitudes. These source FP4 conventions do not reserve IEEE-style infinities/NaNs. [Review, page 97] Practice 7 · Explain a range/precision tradeoff with actual values Constructed question: For the two source codebooks above, which represents 8 exactly? Which represents 2.5 exactly? Which gives a nearer value to 2.9 under nearest rounding? Worked answer: E3M0 represents 8 ; E1M2 represents 2.5 . At 2.9, E1M2 chooses 3, distance 0.1. E3M0 chooses 2, distance 0.9; 4 is farther away at 1.1. E1M2 is closer for this input, but cannot reach 8. One example’s smaller error does not establish the best format for every tensor. The source’s FP8 examples also have their own contracts: E4M3 reaches 448 and has no infinity encoding, while E5M2 reaches 57344 and reserves infinity/NaN patterns. Their field widths alone do not justify copying every FP32 special-case rule. Consult the named format’s convention. [Review, page 96] Quantization replaces a large set of possible values with a discrete codebook The final source page calls the difference between an input and its quantized value quantization error . For intuition, take a constructed grid with spacing 0.5: …,−0.5,0,0.5,1,1.5,… . Under nearest rounding, input 1.1 becomes 1, with signed reconstruction error 1−1.1 = −0.1. Storage saves space because you store a small code identifying a permitted value rather than an unrestricted high-precision input. [Review, page 98] Practice 8 · Connect the codebook to CNN storage Constructed question: A tensor has 864 weights. Compare ideal packed FP32 and 4-bit storage. Then suppose a stated quantizer rounds its weight 1.1 to 1. What is the signed error, and does the storage ratio prove an equal speedup? Worked answer: FP32 stores 864 ×32/8 = 3,456 bytes . Four-bit packing stores 864 ×4/8 = 432 bytes , an 8-fold raw-value storage reduction . The signed error is −0.1 . This assumes packing and excludes scales/metadata. It establishes neither measured speed nor final model accuracy; hardware execution and how the model reacts to changed weights still matter.
